newsitem.title: CANADA: New evidence for black holes presented.
newsitem.headline: New evidence for black holes presented.

text.p: Researchers presented new evidence on Monday that the mysterious astronomical features known as black holes do in fact exist -- but even the scientists who did the research said this was not conclusive proof.

One new shred of evidence involved the presence of "event horizons", one-way membranes surrounding black holes that, once crossed, cut off all contact with the rest of the universe, researchers reported at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society.

Black holes, first posited by Albert Einstein, have been described as the ultimate victory of gravity: they are thought to be unimaginably dense astronomical bodies that have collapsed in on themselves and that then suck in stars and other galactic features.

Scientists at the AAS meeting in Toronto reported on two distinct kinds of black holes: the supermassive kind thought to lie at the heart of immense galaxies and the solar kind believed to draw their matter and energy from one neighbouring star.

In examining solar black holes, scientists at the Harvard- Smithsonian Centre for Astrophysics in Cambridge, Massachusetts, reported on the presence of a one-way membrane called an "event horizon" around the tiny, dense heart of the hole.
Astronomer Ramesh Narayan described the event horizon as "a sort of one-way membrane ... matter and energy can fall in but nothing can get out through the event horizon, not even light."
This means that even before matter and energy are swallowed by a black hole, they are gone forever in the eyes of the universe.

The discovery of event horizons is important, Narayan and other researchers said, because these features are unique to black holes. They do not occur around so-called neutron stars, which are nearly as dense as black holes and also take in vast amounts of energy.
Unlike black holes, which make matter and energy disappear and are consequently invisible to earthly view, neutron stars radiate energy back out into the universe and can be seen as dots of light.
Other researchers, using the orbiting Hubble Space Telescope to focus on supermassive black holes, found three such features in three normal galaxies not far from the Milky Way.
They concluded that such big black holes are so common that nearly every large galaxy has one, and the bigger the galaxy, the bigger its black hole.

These huge black holes -- some with 100 million times the mass of the Sun -- are thought to be the remains of dead quasars, the powerful, super-bright hearts of galaxies. Future research could help clarify quasars' role in galaxy formation and evolution.
This evidence about both kinds of black holes was seen as valuable but only circumstantial by a panel of scientists discussing the findings at a news conference.
"The evidence was strong, but not strong enough to convict in a court of law," said Scott Tremaine of the Canadian Institute for Theoretical Astrophysics.

Douglas Richstone of the University of Michigan had a more prosaic assessment of the new black hole research: "Certainly I wouldn't be prepared to bet everything or even my home on it. But I would be prepared to bet my car on it, and it's not a bad car."
